client: I've been really stressed out lately about my grades — it's my final semester and I feel like everything is riding on how I perform. The other day I overheard some classmates talking about these intense study schedules they have mapped out, and it just made me feel like I'm already falling behind even though the semester barely started. Honestly, I'm not totally sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent worry — and even though your voice stays calm and measured, there's a real weight behind what you're sharing, especially with so much feeling like it's on the line this semester. That moment of overhearing your classmates is a great example of something CBT calls **comparison thinking** — where we use someone else's highlight reel as evidence that we're already failing, even without checking whether that's actually true. I'm really glad you gave this a shot, and I'd love to help you untangle some of those thoughts together — because talking *can* shift things, even when it doesn't feel that way at first.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about the comparison thing, but honestly it doesn't feel like I'm just assuming they're doing better than me — they literally were talking about finishing a project I haven't even started yet. It's hard to call that a distortion when it seems pretty grounded in reality. And I guess I'm a little skeptical that just... talking about it is going to change the fact that I'm behind.
therapist: Your voice tells me this is hitting harder than your words might let on — there's a real urgency and frustration there, and that makes complete sense given what you're describing. You're right that noticing a classmate is ahead on a project is a real, concrete thing — but the part worth examining is the leap from "they started before me" to "I'm already behind and this is a problem," because that leap carries a lot of assumptions about timelines, your own capacity, and what "on track" even means for *you*. The goal isn't to talk away the facts, but to loosen the grip of the story those facts are being used to tell.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it intellectually, but it's really hard to separate the "story" from what feels like just... reality. Like, if someone else is further along, doesn't that objectively mean I have less time than I thought? I guess I'm not sure how to just decide to stop feeling like I'm already losing when the evidence feels so concrete.
therapist: The way you're speaking — that slightly strained, searching quality — tells me this isn't just an intellectual puzzle for you, it's genuinely distressing, and I want to honor that rather than just hand you a reframe. You're absolutely right that CBT isn't about *deciding* to stop feeling something — it's about noticing that "they're further along" and "I'm losing" are actually two separate things, and that second one is where your mind is doing extra work that's costing you energy you need right now. The question isn't whether you're behind someone else, but whether *your* plan, starting now, is enough — and that's something we can actually look at together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that distinction — between "they're ahead" and "I'm losing" — actually matters. But honestly, when I'm lying awake at three in the morning running through everyone else's LinkedIn updates in my head, that separation just doesn't feel real. It's like my brain knows the logical difference but refuses to act like it does.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a real edge of tension — matches exactly what you're describing: your nervous system is already in that 3am place even as we talk, and that's important information. What you're naming is actually one of the most human and frustrating parts of this work — that knowing something logically and *feeling* it as true are processed in completely different parts of us, and insight alone doesn't automatically quiet the alarm. That gap between your thinking brain and your feeling brain is exactly where we'd want to focus — not on convincing yourself harder, but on building small, concrete anchors that give your mind something real to hold onto instead of LinkedIn at 3am.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and honestly it kind of makes sense that my body is doing the thing right now even just talking about it. But when you say "small concrete anchors" — I don't really know what that means in practice, and part of me is skeptical that anything is going to feel real enough at 3am when my brain is already convinced I'm unemployable and falling behind everyone I know. Like, what anchor is going to compete with a LinkedIn feed full of people getting promoted?
therapist: The pitch and pace in your voice right now tells me that skepticism is real and alive — this isn't just an intellectual question, you genuinely need something that can hold up under pressure, and that's a fair demand. A concrete anchor in that moment might look like a single, specific piece of *your own* evidence — not a mantra, but something like a past project you finished when you doubted yourself, something your brain can't as easily argue with the way it can argue with general reassurance. The goal isn't to out-compete LinkedIn, but to give your mind one true, personal thing to return to — because right now it's defaulting to everyone else's story, and we want to start building yours.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I think I understand the idea — find something real, something I actually did, not just a feel-good phrase. But when I try to think of a past project right now, my brain immediately jumps to all the ways it wasn't that impressive, or how someone else did something similar but better. It's like even my own memories get filtered through that same comparison lens before I can even use them as evidence.
therapist: There's something tender in the way you're saying this — soft and careful, like you're handling something fragile — and what you're describing is actually a really significant insight: the comparison filter isn't just about other people, it's rewriting your own history in real time. That's a pattern called **discounting the positive**, where your mind automatically finds a reason why your evidence doesn't count, which means the problem isn't that you lack good memories — it's that they're getting intercepted before they can land. So rather than searching for an impressive achievement, I'd want to ask you something smaller: can you think of a moment where you kept going even when you doubted yourself — not because it went perfectly, but just because you did it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, there is a moment that comes to mind, but I'm already doing that thing you just described — I'm already telling myself it doesn't really count. It was just showing up to a work presentation when I was terrified, shaking the whole time, and I got through it, but my brain immediately goes to "well, you stumbled over your words twice and someone else would have done it better." I can see the pattern you're naming, but knowing about it doesn't make it stop happening — it's like I can watch myself discount it and still not be able to catch it in time.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me something just shifted — like part of you recognized something real in that memory even as another part rushed to take it away, and that tension is actually meaningful. But I want to stay with what you just described for a second: you were terrified, shaking, and you walked in anyway and got through it — that's not a small thing, that's evidence of someone who acts despite fear, which is exactly the muscle you're going to need this semester. The fact that you can *see* the discounting happening is actually the first crack in its power — you're not failing to catch it, you're catching it in slow motion, and that's where the work begins.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it, but then there's this other voice that immediately says "that was just one time, it doesn't count as a pattern." Like, I caught myself discounting just now as you were talking, which is kind of what you meant, but it almost feels like the discounting is faster than I am. And honestly, the idea that I have this "muscle" for acting despite fear sounds good in theory, but this semester feels so much bigger than one presentation — there are so many more chances to fall apart.
therapist: There's something striking happening right now — your voice is soft and fast, like you're thinking out loud and almost afraid to land on anything too firmly, and yet you just did something really significant: you caught the discounting voice mid-sentence, in real time, which means you *are* faster than you think. One presentation doesn't need to be the whole pattern — it just needs to be the first data point, and this semester will give you more, not more chances to fall apart, but more chances to add to that evidence. The voice that says "it doesn't count" is loud, but it's not the only voice in the room anymore — and that's worth noticing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it, like there's a small flicker of something when you put it that way. But then I think, okay, I caught the voice once, in here, where it feels safer to notice things — what happens when I'm standing up there in front of everyone and my mind goes blank and there's no one to slow me down? I guess I'm just not sure one moment of catching it in a therapy session translates to being able to do it when the stakes actually feel real.
therapist: That very high, soft, quick quality in your voice right now feels like someone standing at the edge of something — there's a flicker of hope you're almost afraid to touch, and I want to be careful with it too. But here's what's worth holding onto: the goal isn't to be perfectly calm in that high-stakes moment, it's to have caught the voice *enough times* in lower-stakes moments that it becomes even slightly more familiar when it shows up under pressure — you're essentially practicing the muscle here so it's a little less foreign when you need it. And you've already done the hardest version of this once — shaking, terrified, in front of people — so the question isn't whether you can handle it, it's whether you can start trusting that the person who walked into that presentation is the same person walking into this semester.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe it. But I keep thinking... that presentation felt like a fluke, like I somehow got lucky and held it together just barely enough, and I'm not sure that counts as proof that I can do it again. What if the next time is the time it all actually falls apart?
therapist: That very high, soft quality in your voice — almost like you're holding your breath — tells me this "what if it falls apart" thought carries a lot of weight, and I want to name what I'm noticing: you've now described the same presentation as "just showing up," then "getting through it," then "barely holding it together," and now "a fluke" — each time your mind finds a new way to make it smaller. That's not evidence that it was a fluke; that's the discounting pattern working overtime to protect you from trusting yourself, because trusting yourself feels riskier than staying braced for failure. What if "barely holding it together" is actually just what courage looks like from the inside?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
